This document covers REGULATION (EU) No 530/2012 OF THE EUROPEAN PARLIAMENT AND OF THE COUNCIL of 13 June 2012 on the accelerated phasing-in of double-hull or equivalent design requirements for single-hull oil tankers (recast). It is a Union regulation for the shipping of oil, and it sets conditions on the tankers that may fly a Member State flag or call at a Union port or offshore terminal. This Regulation shall be binding in its entirety and directly applicable in all Member States.

## 2. What This Regulation Is and Why It Applies to the Workspace

The purpose of this Regulation is to establish an accelerated phasing-in scheme for the application of the double-hull or equivalent design requirements of MARPOL 73/78, as defined in Article 3 of this Regulation, to single-hull oil tankers, and to ban the transport to or from ports of the Member States of heavy grade oil in single-hull oil tankers. This Regulation shall apply to oil tankers of 5 000 tonnes deadweight and above: (a) which fly the flag of a Member State; (b) irrespective of their flag, which enter or leave a port or offshore terminal or anchor in an area under the jurisdiction of a Member State. For operators of ocean freight, the Regulation sets a condition on the tonnage a carrier may deploy to Union ports: a single-hull oil tanker is not a lawful call, whatever its flag.

*Operational implication:* operators chartering or contracting tonnage for oil and heavy grade oil cargoes into Union ports confirm the hull design of each vessel before the fixture is agreed.

## 3. Issues Requiring Immediate Action

MONITORING: no immediate action is needed for operators whose oil cargoes already move on double-hull tonnage. The remaining decision is contractual: a chartering desk adds a hull-design statement to every voyage charter and carrier booking for oil cargo into a Union port. Exceptions exist but cannot be planned around: By way of derogation from Articles 4, 5 and 7, the competent authority of a Member State may, subject to national provisions, allow, under exceptional circumstances, an individual ship to enter or leave a port or offshore terminal or anchor in an area under the jurisdiction of that Member State, when: (a) an oil tanker is in difficulty and in search of a place of refuge; (b) an unloaded oil tanker is proceeding to a port of repair.

*Legal Confirmation Required:* whether a given vessel falls inside an exception is for counsel and the competent authority of the port State.

## 4. How the Workspace Sits in the Compliance Chain

The Regulation binds vessels, flag States and port States, and it places one explicit duty on Member States. Each Member State shall inform the IMO of its decision to deny entry to oil tankers, pursuant to Article 7 of this Regulation, operating in accordance with Regulation 20.5 of Annex I to MARPOL 73/78 into the ports or offshore terminals under its jurisdiction, on the basis of Regulation 20.8.2 of Annex I to MARPOL 73/78.

A forwarder or non-vessel operating carrier that books oil cargo is not named as a duty holder; the practical exposure is a booking that cannot be performed because the contracted vessel is refused entry. *Legal Confirmation Required:* whether a forwarder arranging a voyage charter carries any contractual liability for a refused vessel depends on the charter terms and is for counsel.

## 6. Anticipated Authoritative Guidance and Pending Regulatory Events

The Regulation gives the Commission a limited rulemaking power: The Commission shall be empowered to adopt delegated acts in accordance with Article 11 concerning the alignment of the references in this Regulation to the non-substantial amendments, such as renumbering, adopted by the IMO to the Regulations of Annex I to MARPOL 73/78. The period of the power is stated as follows: The power to adopt the delegated acts referred to in Article 10(1) shall be conferred on the Commission for a period of five years from 20 July 2012. The stored source dates no delegated act, so no act is scheduled on the evidence held. The power is limited to alignment of references and does not widen the scope of the Regulation.

## 8. Substantive Requirements

### Double-hull condition

Cause: No oil tanker shall be allowed to operate under the flag of a Member State, nor shall any oil tanker, irrespective of its flag, be allowed to enter into ports or offshore terminals under the jurisdiction of a Member State unless such tanker is a double-hull oil tanker.

Mechanical consequence: a vessel that is not a double-hull oil tanker cannot be flagged in a Member State or call at a Union port or offshore terminal.

Effect by vertical: the stored source states no cargo-vertical difference; effect on each cargo vertical needs carrier-specific data.

### Heavy grade oil

Cause: No oil tanker carrying heavy grade oil, irrespective of its flag, shall be allowed to enter or leave ports or offshore terminals or to anchor in areas under the jurisdiction of a Member State, unless such tanker is a double-hull oil tanker.

Mechanical consequence: the double-hull condition applies to heavy grade oil carriage in every case.

Effect by vertical: effect on each cargo vertical needs carrier-specific data.

### Condition Assessment Scheme

Cause: Irrespective of its flag, a single-hull oil tanker above 15 years of age shall not be allowed to enter or leave ports or offshore terminals or anchor in areas under the jurisdiction of a Member State unless such tanker complies with the Condition Assessment Scheme referred to in Article 6.

Mechanical consequence: an older single-hull tanker needs a compliant Condition Assessment Scheme record to call.

Effect by vertical: effect on each cargo vertical needs carrier-specific data.

### Final date

Cause: After the anniversary of the date of delivery of the ship in 2015, the following shall no longer be allowed: the entry into the ports or offshore terminals under the jurisdiction of a Member State of other Category 2 and Category 3 oil tankers, irrespective of the fact that they continue to operate under the flag of a third State in accordance with Regulation 20.5 of Annex I to MARPOL 73/78.

Mechanical consequence: the 2015 date is past, so Category 2 and Category 3 tankers can no longer continue under a third State flag into Union ports.

*Legal Confirmation Required:* the application of the categories to a given vessel is for counsel and the flag State.

No phase-in is stated in Articles 4 to 7 beyond the final date above.
No exceptions are stated in Articles 4 to 7 other than those in Article 8, covered in section 12.
No scope limits are stated in Articles 1 to 3 other than the deadweight thresholds above.

## 10. Registration and Reporting Obligations

The only reporting duty in the stored source falls on Member States, not on operators. Each Member State shall inform the IMO of its decision to deny entry to oil tankers, pursuant to Article 7 of this Regulation, operating in accordance with Regulation 20.5 of Annex I to MARPOL 73/78 into the ports or offshore terminals under its jurisdiction, on the basis of Regulation 20.8.2 of Annex I to MARPOL 73/78. No registration scheme for operators is stated.

## 11. Operational System Requirements

MONITORING: the Regulation asks operators for no system build. A chartering desk adds a hull-design field and, for a single-hull vessel above 15 years of age, a Condition Assessment Scheme status field to the vessel record, and completes both before an oil cargo booking is confirmed.

## 12. Exemptions and Edge Cases

By way of derogation from Articles 4, 5 and 7, the competent authority of a Member State may, subject to national provisions, allow, under exceptional circumstances, an individual ship to enter or leave a port or offshore terminal or anchor in an area under the jurisdiction of that Member State, when: (a) an oil tanker is in difficulty and in search of a place of refuge; (b) an unloaded oil tanker is proceeding to a port of repair. Oil tankers operated exclusively in ports and inland navigation may be exempted from paragraph 3 provided that they are duly certified under inland waterway legislation.

This document covers COUNCIL DECISION (EU) 2021/594 of 9 April 2021 on the position to be taken on behalf of the European Union within the European Committee for drawing up standards in the field of inland navigation and within the Central Commission for the Navigation of the Rhine on the adoption of standards concerning professional qualifications in inland navigation. It is an act of the Council of the European Union that fixes how the Union votes inside two inland navigation bodies. It sets no duty on freight operators. The Union is not a member of the CCNR or of CESNI. The Union’s position should therefore be expressed by the Member States that are members of those bodies, acting jointly in the interests of the Union.

## 2. What This Regulation Is and Why It Applies to the Workspace

The Decision fixes two positions: The position to be taken on the Union’s behalf within CESNI with regard to the adoption of CESNI standard 20_04 and CESNI standard 20_39 shall be to agree to their adoption. The second position concerns the Rhine commission: The position to be taken on the Union’s behalf within the CCNR with regard to the adoption of a resolution amending the Regulations for Rhine Navigation Personnel in order to include a reference to the ES-QIN standards, including CESNI standard 20_04 and CESNI standard 20_39, shall be to support all proposals aligning the requirements of the Regulations for the Rhine Navigation Personnel with the ES-QIN standards. The Decision is a voting position, not a crew or vessel rule.

*Operational implication:* a forwarder that books Rhine inland waterway legs relies on the barge operator's crew qualification regime; the standards named in this Decision concern that regime, and the Decision itself changes no booking condition.

## 3. Issues Requiring Immediate Action

MONITORING: no immediate action is required of freight operators. The Decision is an internal Union voting position, and CESNI standard 20_04 and CESNI standard 20_39 aim to contribute to maintaining the highest level of safety in inland navigation and would encourage harmonisation in the context of Directive (EU) 2017/2397.

## 4. How the Workspace Sits in the Compliance Chain

The Decision binds the Member States that sit in the two bodies, which express the Union position jointly: The position set out in Article 1(1) shall be expressed by the Member States that are members of the CESNI, acting jointly in the interests of the Union. A forwarder or shipper is not named as a duty holder. *Legal Confirmation Required:* whether any later national crew qualification rule that follows these standards reaches a forwarder's contracts is for counsel.

Purpose and Scope of This Document

This document covers a Ministry of Oceans and Fisheries announcement titled "S. Korea implements 0.10% sulphur limit on vessels at anchorage or mooring in its five major ports". It is a ministry press release that reports a national marine fuel standard for the designated Emission Control Areas of South Korea. It reports the standard and its legal basis; it is not the text of the notice itself.

## 2. What This Regulation Is and Why It Applies to the Workspace

The announcement states: On 1 September 2020, a new marine fuel standard, SOx Emission Control Area regulation, will enter into force. The SOX Emission Control Area regulation (Public notice No. 2019-202 by the Ministry of Oceans and Fisheries) is enacted in accordance with Article 10 of the Special Act on the Improvement of Air Quality in Port Areas, etc. For ocean freight operators the standard sets the fuel a vessel burns while it is in the five port areas, so it bears on carrier fuel choice for calls at those ports.

*Operational implication:* carriers calling these ports choose between low-sulphur fuel and an exhaust cleaning system; a forwarder asks which route each carrier has chosen before a surcharge is agreed.

## 3. Issues Requiring Immediate Action

MONITORING: the first phase began on 1 September 2020 and the second phase began in January 2022, so both dates are before the date of this brief. No immediate step is open for carriers already compliant. The step that remains is a check: a fuel-compliance lead confirms that each carrier serving Busan, Incheon, Yeosu-Gwangyang, Ulsan or Pyeongtaek-Dangjin burns fuel at or below the limit or runs an exhaust cleaning system that meets the stated ratio, and that the change-over record is logged. The release states the limit as follows: must use fuel with a sulphur content of no more than 0.10% from 1 September 2020, against the current limit of 0.50%.

*Legal Confirmation Required:* how the limit and the alternative route apply to a given vessel call is for counsel and the port State.

## 4. How the Workspace Sits in the Compliance Chain

The release addresses vessels in the Emission Control Areas and their operators. A forwarder or shipper is not named as a duty holder. *Analytical inference:* any exposure is indirect, through a carrier that passes fuel or exhaust cleaning cost into a surcharge on calls at these ports; the release states a fuel standard and no surcharge, so any surcharge is a carrier decision that the release does not describe.

Cause: must use fuel with a sulphur content of no more than 0.10% from 1 September 2020, against the current limit of 0.50%.

From January 2022 onward, the scope will be expanded to include all vessels entering the ECAs.

Mechanical consequence: from the second phase the limit covers every vessel entering the areas, not only vessels at anchorage or berth.

What's Moving and What Triggered It

Signal event: Prices for natural gas in Europe and Asia have diverged from those in the United States since the February 28 closure of the Strait of Hormuz . Futures prices for liquified natural gas (LNG) delivery to the Title Transfer Facility (TTF), the European benchmark price, increased to $14.80 per million British thermal units (MMBtu) for the week ending April 24, 35% higher than before the closure, according to data from Bloomberg L.P. In East Asia, the front-month futures price for the benchmark Japan-Korea Marker (JKM), rose 51% over the same period to $16.02/MMBtu. In contrast, natural gas prices at the U.S. benchmark Henry Hub have decreased 9% since February 28 due to limited opportunities for increasing LNG exports in the near term and ample domestic seasonal natural gas storage and supply . The closure of the strait has affected over 10 billion cubic feet per day (Bcf/d) of global LNG supplies, or approximately 20% , mostly from Qatar’s Ras Laffan export facility. No laden LNG vessels are known to have crossed the strait between March 1 and April 24, according to Kpler data.

For context on the US side, In 2025, the wholesale U.S. natural gas spot price at the national benchmark Henry Hub in Louisiana averaged $3.52 per million British thermal units (MMBtu), based on data from LSEG Data. ## 2. Who's Driving It and What They Want

Driving parties: QatarEnergy declared force majeure on March 4, which has forced Asian buyers who import over 80% of Qatari gas to compete for spot cargoes on global markets to replace lost contract volumes. The US Department of Energy is the other named party: Since the closure, the U.S. Department of Energy has approved two increases to terminal export authorizations to countries lacking free trade agreements (FTAs) with the United States since February The source states no wish or strategy for any party beyond these actions. It adds a limit on US supply: The export terminal capacity utilization in March amounted to 94% of the maximum DOE-approved export levels, according to our most recent Short-Term Energy Outlook and Liquefaction Capacity File .

## 3. Expected Trajectory and Conversion Triggers

We expect U.S. LNG exports will increase, but only by a small portion of the missing volumes. In the same analysis, we expect that approximately 2.4 Bcf/d of DOE-authorized export capacity will come online between April and December 2026. Whether that capacity came online is not in the stored source, which is dated April 28, 2026. Although average weekly TTF prices have fallen from a three-year high reached in mid-March, prices remain elevated compared with February. Asian natural gas storage capacity is less than European capacity, and JKM prices are likely to move with weather-related spot demand.

Conversion trigger: the stored source names no price level or event that moves the signal from observation to commercial pressure on carrier fuel surcharges, and it holds no freight rate. *Analytical inference:* a sustained gap between the European and East Asian benchmarks and the US benchmark would raise LNG cost for any fuel buyer priced off those benchmarks, but the source does not say so.

What the Research Found

Headline finding: With the current level of policy action, CO 2 emissions are projected to be between 729-768 MtCO 2 in 2030 (based on a voyage-based approach), only representing a 1-6% decrease below the reference emissions level in 2008. The CAT rates 2030 emissions under current policies as “Highly Insufficient.”

**Population:** international shipping. International shipping accounts for about 2.3% of global CO 2 emissions in 2023 (ICCT, 2025).

**Intervention:** the policy measures of the International Maritime Organization as they stand. The IMO failed to adopt the Net Zero Framework (NZF), a global fuel standard and carbon pricing mechanism, at the Marine Environment Protection Committee’s (MEPC) extraordinary session in October 2025.

**Comparator:** the reference emissions level in 2008 stated in the headline finding, and the IMO emissions target: Current policies put the shipping sector far off track from achieving the IMO’s target of reducing emissions by 20% and striving for 30% by 2030, with an implementation gap of 109–186 MtCO 2 .

**Outcome:** a 1 to 6 percent decrease below the 2008 level in 2030 under current policy, in the headline finding above; the absolute figure is the range in MtCO 2 given there. There remains an ambition gap of 78-87% between current policy projections and 1.5°C compatible pathways for 2030.

**Methodology in brief, scope and limitations:** These are the main policy measures underpinning the CAT’s current policy projections. The rating is by the Climate Action Tracker, stated in its own words: The CAT rates 2030 emissions under current policies as “Highly Insufficient.” The rating remains unchanged from the previous assessment since no new policy measures have been adopted that would reduce emissions projections. Evidence grade: not assigned; the stored text holds no maturity assessment and no peer review statement, and no inferred grade is given.

## 2. Why This Finding Matters Operationally and Commercially

Cause: The IMO failed to adopt the Net Zero Framework (NZF), a global fuel standard and carbon pricing mechanism, at the Marine Environment Protection Committee’s (MEPC) extraordinary session in October 2025.

Mechanical consequence: The rating remains unchanged from the previous assessment since no new policy measures have been adopted that would reduce emissions projections.

The page names the most recent ship efficiency measures: The most recent measures, Energy Efficiency of Existing Ship Index (EEXI) and the Carbon Intensity Indicator (CII), came into effect in January 2023, with the first ratings and reporting issued in 2024 (Infineum Insight, 2025).

Effect by vertical: the page addresses international shipping as a whole and states no cargo-vertical effect; the effect on each vertical needs carrier-specific data. *Analytical inference:* ocean carriers with rated vessels may face vessel-level efficiency plans, because the page states: Ships rated E, or rated as D for three consecutive years, will need to develop a plan to increase their operational efficiency (DNV, 2023). The page does not say how that reaches charter selection.

## 3. What the Finding Changes for Strategy, Claims, or Decisions

What the Research Found

Headline finding: Passenger and freight travel account for 28% of U.S. greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions today. We explore pathways to reduce transportation emissions using NREL’s TEMPO model under bounding assumptions on future travel behavior, technology advancement, and policies. Results show diverse routes to 80% or more well-to-wheel GHG reductions by 2050.

The source's own language on who published the finding: it appears as Nat Commun . 2023 Oct 30;14:6913. with authors at the National Renewable Energy Laboratory, Golden, CO USA and at the U.S. Department of Energy. It reports model scenarios, not forecasts.

**Population:** passenger and freight mobility in the United States, including freight trucks and aviation fuel use.

**Intervention:** a set of technology, fuel, policy and travel behaviour assumptions, run through a national transportation model: simulating 2173 long-term scenarios focusing on the impacts of different technologies, fuels, policies, and changes in travel behavior and choices guided by expert elicitation.

**Comparator:** a baseline aligned to a national reference case. In the baseline scenario, emissions are reduced by 24% relative to 2019

**Outcome:** in the median scenario, zero-emission vehicle sales reach 89% for passenger light-duty and 69% for freight trucks by 2030 and 100% sales for both by 2040. Up to 3,000 terawatt-hours of electricity could be needed in 2050 to power plug-in electric vehicles. Increased sustainable biofuel usage is also essential for decarbonizing aviation (10–42 billion gallons needed in 2050) and to support legacy vehicles during the transition.

**Methodology in brief, scope and limitations:** the authors state the bounds: the model runs under bounding assumptions, and one test of 172 scenarios in which one input was varied at a time and all others held constant to the baseline. Currently, few high-resolution models exist that capture the transportation system collectively with the ability to represent new technology and mobility solutions to inform decision makers and investments Evidence grade: not assigned; the stored text holds no maturity assessment beyond journal acceptance, and no inferred grade is given.

## 2. Why This Finding Matters Operationally and Commercially

Cause: Rapid adoption of zero-emission vehicles coupled with a clean electric grid is essential for deep decarbonization

Mechanical consequence: in the median scenario, zero-emission vehicle sales reach 89% for passenger light-duty and 69% for freight trucks by 2030 and 100% sales for both by 2040.

Effect by vertical: the study covers passenger and freight mobility in aggregate and states no cargo-vertical effect; the effect on each vertical needs carrier-specific data. *Analytical inference:* road carriers that plan fleet renewal around the median scenario would face the 2030 freight truck share stated above, and the study gives it as a scenario result and not as a market forecast.

## 3. What the Finding Changes for Strategy, Claims, or Decisions

The finding limits one claim and supports a planning view. An operator cannot cite the 2030 and 2040 sales shares as a prediction, because they are the median of modelled scenarios under bounding assumptions. The planning view in the authors' words: Rapid adoption of zero-emission vehicles coupled with a clean electric grid is essential for deep decarbonization; and Managing travel demand growth can ease this transition by reducing the need for clean electricity and sustainable fuels.
